acceptedAnswer.text: Once enamel has been lost through acid erosion, it cannot be regenerated by the body. However, the effects of erosion can be managed and the remaining tooth structure protected. In cases of early or mild erosion, fluoride treatments and dietary modifications may help slow progression. Where enamel has been significantly thinned or lost, composite bonding can be applied to cover exposed surfaces, reduce sensitivity, and restore the tooth's natural shape. The most appropriate approach depends on the extent of damage and should be determined through a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last on eroded teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding on eroded teeth may typically last between five and ten years, though longevity varies depending on several factors. The location of the bonding, dietary habits, oral hygiene, and whether the underlying cause of erosion has been managed all influence how long the restoration lasts. Teeth subject to ongoing acid exposure or heavy biting forces may experience wear on the bonding more quickly. Composite bonding can be repaired or replaced when needed, and your dentist will monitor its condition during routine check-ups to advise on maintenance as appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Is composite bonding suitable for severe enamel erosion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding is generally well suited to cases of mild to moderate acid erosion where some tooth structure remains intact. For teeth with more extensive damage — where significant enamel and dentine have been lost, or where structural integrity is compromised — alternative restorative options such as porcelain veneers or dental crowns may offer more durable and protective solutions. Your dentist will assess the severity of erosion and the condition of the remaining tooth structure during a clinical examination before recommending the most appropriate treatment approach for your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: Does composite bonding prevent further acid erosion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding provides a physical barrier over the treated tooth surface, which can help protect the underlying dentine from direct acid contact. However, bonding does not make teeth immune to further erosion. The composite material itself can be affected by prolonged acid exposure over time. For this reason, managing the source of acid — whether through dietary changes, treatment for acid reflux, or other measures — remains essential alongside any restorative work. A combined approach of bonding and preventative management generally offers the most favourable long-term outcome.

mainEntity.name: Will bonding for acid erosion look natural?

acceptedAnswer.text: Modern composite resin materials are available in a wide range of shades and translucencies, allowing your dentist to closely match the bonding to the colour and appearance of your natural teeth. The material is applied in layers and carefully sculpted to recreate natural tooth contours and surface texture. Once polished, composite bonding can often blend closely with the surrounding teeth. Your dentist will take time to match the shade carefully during the procedure to ensure the most natural-looking result possible for your individual tooth colour and characteristics.

Yes, acid erosion can affect children and adolescents as well as adults. Frequent consumption of fruit juices, fizzy drinks, and acidic snacks are common contributing factors in younger patients. Children's enamel is also thinner and less mineralised than adult enamel, which may make it more vulnerable to acid attack. If you notice changes in the appearance of your child's teeth — such as thinning, yellowing, or increased sensitivity — it may be worth arranging a dental assessment. Early identification allows for dietary advice and preventative measures to be put in place before significant damage occurs.
